title: Second Treatise of Government
author: John Locke
openingChapterLabel: Chapter 1 — An Essay Concerning the True Original, Extent and End of Civil Government
openingText: In the previous discourse I have shown:
about:
What gives anyone the right to rule another person? Locke begins from natural freedom and equality. Political authority must rest on consent and serve the preservation of life, liberty, and property. Government therefore has limits, including limits on what it may do in the name of law.

The book opens by summarizing the preceding treatise's rejection of royal authority derived from Adam. It then examines the state of nature, property, parental power, consent, and the organization of government. The later chapters distinguish legitimate authority from conquest, usurpation, and tyranny.

Watch the qualifications attached to the principles. Labour can establish property, but Locke also discusses limits on appropriation and the effects of money. Express and tacit consent do not create exactly the same relationship to a community. Resistance, in turn, is not a licence to overthrow government for every mistake. The argument draws on reason, biblical examples, and quotations from other writers.

angleCards.title: Freedom under natural law
angleCards.text: The state of nature has no common political superior, but it is not a condition without rules. Locke distinguishes it from the state of war and uses natural law to limit what people may do to one another.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track the distinction between the state of nature and the state of war, and ask why naturally free people form political societies.

angleCards.title: Labour, property, and money
angleCards.text: Chapter 5 explains how labour can make something held in common into private property. Follow the requirement to leave enough for others, the limit imposed by spoilage, and the introduction of money.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how Locke's justification of property relates to its initial limits and to the inequality made possible by money.

angleCards.title: What counts as consent?
angleCards.text: Locke distinguishes express membership in a society from the tacit consent involved in using its territory and protection. Notice the different obligations and relationships these create.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the arguments about consent and majority decisions, and assess whether they explain an individual's obligation to obey.

angleCards.title: When may the people resist?
angleCards.text: The final chapters ask what happens when rulers use authority against its purpose. Locke distinguishes individual mistakes from a continuing attempt to subject the people to arbitrary power.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Chapter 19 for the specific conditions that justify resistance and for Locke's account of who may judge whether they have been met.

cast.name: John Locke
cast.description: Locke examines political authority as a trust. His argument moves from natural freedom to the formation of society and then to the circumstances in which government loses its claim to obedience.

cast.name: Robert Filmer
cast.description: The first chapter summarizes the rejection of Filmer's account of royal authority through Adam and paternal power. Locke then seeks a different explanation of political authority.

cast.name: The State of Nature
cast.description: People are naturally free and equal but remain subject to natural law. Without a common judge, disagreement and partiality can make their rights insecure.

cast.name: Property
cast.description: Locke examines the origin of property through labour. In several passages he also uses property broadly to include people's lives, liberties, and possessions.

cast.name: Consent
cast.description: Consent forms free individuals into a political community. Locke examines majority rule and distinguishes express consent from the tacit consent involved in enjoying a government's territory and protection.

cast.name: The Legislative Power
cast.description: The legislature is the supreme authority within government, but it must follow natural law and work for the preservation of society. It has no right arbitrarily to destroy those it exists to protect.

whyItMatters.title: Power needs justification
whyItMatters.body: Locke distinguishes possessing power from having a right to exercise it. Conquest, inherited rank, and physical strength do not by themselves supply the political authority he seeks to justify.

whyItMatters.title: Freedom and common rules
whyItMatters.body: The book examines a problem raised by its own starting point: how can naturally free people become bound by collective decisions? Consent, majority rule, and established laws are different parts of Locke's answer.

whyItMatters.title: Limits on government
whyItMatters.body: Government must preserve what people established it to protect. Resistance therefore becomes part of the argument about legitimate authority. Locke nevertheless distinguishes ordinary mistakes from serious breaches of the trust placed in rulers.
